In developing the look of the smart-mouthed superhero, production designer Sean Haworth and his team drew inspiration from the wide range of artists and writers behind the popular comics. "Rob Liefeld drew the definitive Deadpool," Tim Miller said. "People fall in love with something for a reason, and to try and change its fundamental core values is a bad idea. The morally gray area in which Deadpool operates proved particularly appealing to the first-time director. "Deadpool is a guy who's made a lot of bad choices," Miller remarked, iand his screwed-up life is the result. His cynicism, black humor, and sheer insanity distinguish him from other comic book characters. Humor is his main defense - but the guns and swords help! He's always been a very different kind of character than the squeaky-clean heroes in most comic booksi In Deadpool, cancer-ridden former Special Forces operative Wade Wilson (Ryan Reynolds) seeks help from a shadowy government establishment known as Weapon X. DEADPOOL The production photographed car interiors on a soundstage in front of a greenscreen. To mitigate the notoriously difficult task of creating convincing moving vehicle composites from stage photography - and inspired by the immersive lightbox employed to shoot the actors in Gravity - Jonathan Rothbart and Ken Seng decided to replace conventional stage lights with LED panels. "We first shot background plates with a pretty extensive rig," said Rothbart. "We had a seven-camera rig for the freeway, and a fivecamera rig when we were around towni Shooting of the car interiors took place at the tail end of principal photography, to accommodate the time needed to prepare the background plates for use with the LED panels. We had to shoot the plates enough in advance to give me time to set up all of the angles," said Rothbart. "I worked with editorial to tile them, make sure they were in sync, choose which angles would work for each particular sequence, then hand those over to the lighting rig guys." On the greenscreen stage, Seng suspended nine LED panels, each measuring approximately three by four feet, above and around the vehicle buck. Technicians then replayed the background footage through the panels, syncing the content to match the action of the performers inside the vehicle. "While we were shooting," said Rothbart, "I would say, 'This is where they go through the overpass,' or 'Now they're out in the sun,' and we would play the appropriate loop. In addition to accurately lighting the set, the LED panels generated realistic reflections within the vehicle. "We got all this great interaction," noted Rothbart, "on the 17 / 36 leather, on the actors' faces, in the reflections in the chrome - all the subtle activity

that really sells the shot.i DEADPOOL Rothbart and Griggs awarded the majority of the car interior composites - some 90 shots - to Ollin VFX, which had already provided postvis for several hundred shots across the rest of the film. "Postvis is a really interesting process," said Ollin visual effects supervisor Charlie Iturriaga. You help the filmmakers to finish the editing by providing rough comps that are not really very rough at all!" The postvis methodology kickstarted the process of creating the vehicle composites. "We took the background plates, picked the right angles and timings, and got approval from the director and editor," Iturriaga explained. With the backgrounds selected, Ollin composited them with foreground elements, which they further augmented to ensure seamless interaction with the plates, and incorporated digital characters provided by other vendors.iWe added a lot of interactive lighting and reflections inside the cars. We shared assets and plates with Weta, who were in charge of the facial expressions on Deadpool. It was a lot of back and forth - an orchestration between the actual plate, the lighting, the performance animation by others, and us finishing the comps in Nukei On some occasions, the close quarters of the vehicle interiors meant that Reynolds was unable to wear the twin katanas carried by Deadpool on his back. In these instances, Ollin used Maya to model CG swords, which they tracked to the live-action and incorporated into their final composites. Q&A: Eric Durst Gods of Egypt INTERVIEW BY GRAHAM EDWARDS scholars and storytellers alike. Digging deep into this enduring treasure trove of desert lore, Gods of Egypt is an action-adventure filled to the brim with gods and monsters, and is arguably Lionsgate's most ambitious feature to date. When the cruel god Set (Gerard Butler) overthrows his adversary, Horus (Nikolaj Coster-Waldau), the thwarted god finds himself teamed with an unlikely ally in the form of the mortal Bek (Brenton Thwaites). Journeying between realms and battling monstrous creatures, the mismatched duo learns the true meaning of sacrifice in the quest to restore the throne of Egypt to its rightful owner. Director Alex Proyas (The Crow, Dark City, 1, Robot, Knowing) shot the vast majority of Gods of Egypt on stages at Fox Studios Australia, in Sydney, where the actors performed in bluescreen environments with minimal set pieces. Production visual effects supervisor Eric Durst and visual effects producer Jack Geist coordinated the development of around 2,550 visual effects by more than a dozen vendors worldwide.

GODS OF EGYPTI Speaking with Cinetex, Durst discussed his experience of bringing the mythical world of Gods of Egypt fully to life, including the singular challenges posed by the need to portray multiple characters of differing size, not just in a handful of shots, but across most of the film. Eric, you shot Gods of Egypt almost entirely against bluescreen. That must have made previs particularly important. Yes. The previs was done by Proot, Inc., and David Peers was previs supervisor. On a show this size, you really have to previsualize it from the get-go. We had a lot of shots, and limited sets, so we had to really plan it out. On a stage in Sydney, we set up a grid system that was very much like a checkerboard, with A-B-C-D and so on down one side, and 1-2-3-4 down the other, and we set up multiple cameras to capture this whole volume. We had stand-in actors there so Alex could block things out, just as you would a stage play. How did Alex take to that way of working? He immediately gravitated to it. He would come in, block out a sequence very quickly - in a half hour or an hour - then go to the next one, and then the next. In the computer, we would replicate the grid system, and block out all the figures of our main characters, in very rough environments. We used keyframe animation because it's just so fast, and you can make changes so quickly. So, within a day or two, we would have something to show Alex. 2 / 11| Did you previs the entire movie this way?

GODS OF EGYPT We got close. We had about 75 percent of the film ready before we started production, and we carried on with the previs team throughout. Alex had been working on a show called Paradise Lost previous to this, and a lot of the work on it was Avatar-like. But, with Gods of Egypt, we had so many shots, and we had to be so nimble, that even though Alex was very comfortable with the motion capture process, it was just too heavy for this kind of work. GODS OF EGYPT As Nikolaj is changing from his god-self into his falcon-self, we would have him take a deep breath, and do an aggressive move. The same with Gerard Butler and his jackal form. We wanted to get a sense that it took effort to become that other creature. Then we would hand off to animation. We went back and forth on how much of the actor to show when the creature had dialogue. The falcon, especially, was tough to do, because it's got a solid beak, and when it starts to talk it just looks goofy. So we decided to have an intermediate form where the character has the body of a falcon, but it's the actor's head. Did you use motion capture to drive the animation? When we had the actor's head and the body of the creature, that was all rotomated. He would do the performance, and we had witness cameras around, and then the animators - in this case mainly Tippett Studio - would rotomate the performance and then apply that to their animation. We didn't use any motion capture, per se. How about the really gigantic creatures, like the cobras? We had actresses playing the goddesses, riding on their backs. They were on these gimbal mounts. Julian Dimsey at Iloura took their performance and incorporated it into the animation. We had digi-doubles of the characters, as well - sometimes they were hand-offs, and sometimes they were complete digi-double figures, especially when the snakes move erratically. The Sphinx is another giant creature. What did you do for that character? We had an actor who did the facial performance and the voice. Tippett Studio did 10 / 11 the animation, then they gave that to Rising Sun, who did a fabulous job of making this

GODS OF EGYPT creature look as if it was made of sand, so that his moves broke the surface of the face, which would then reform. With over 2,500 shots of gods and monsters, and sun-drenched Ancient Egyptian environments, is there any easy way to sum up this movie? It's a buddy movie, really, with this great Indiana Jones kind of vibe. It also shows mythological characters as the original superheroes, I guess. Only without spandex suits.
